# 12-Week Upper-Body Strength Programme
### Client Profile: 29-year-old recreational climber | Right subacromial impingement | 4 months physio | Cleared for pain-free range, no overhead loading

---

## Guiding Principles Before You Begin

**Communication with her physio is non-negotiable.** Before week one, obtain written confirmation of her current pain-free range of motion, any specific movements to avoid beyond overhead loading, and a shared check-in schedule — ideally at weeks 4 and 8. Everything below is built around the information you have provided, but her physio's guidance supersedes any detail in this plan.

**Pain monitoring protocol.** Use a 0–10 numeric pain scale at the start of every session and before each new exercise. A score of 0–1 is acceptable to proceed. A score of 2 or above means that exercise is modified or removed that day. Any sharp, catching, or radiating pain stops the set immediately. Log scores every session.

**Right-side loading asymmetry.** In the early phases, the right side will be loaded conservatively below the left. This is intentional. As her physio clears greater range and tolerance, you will bring the sides into parity progressively.

---

## Programme Architecture

| Phase | Weeks | Primary Goal |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 – Foundation & Tissue Tolerance | 1–4 | Scapular control, rotator cuff endurance, re-establishing pulling patterns |
| Phase 2 – Hypertrophy & Pattern Loading | 5–8 | Progressive load through horizontal push/pull, grip and forearm development for climbing |
| Phase 3 – Strength Integration | 9–12 | Heavier compound loading, unilateral strength, return-to-climbing preparation |

**Weekly session structure:** Three upper-body sessions per week, separated by at least one rest day. Label them Session A, Session B, and Session C. She may continue lower-body training and cardiovascular work on off days at her and her physio's discretion — this programme does not programme those elements.

---

## PHASE 1 — Foundation & Tissue Tolerance (Weeks 1–4)

### Phase 1 Goals
Establish scapular stability and rotator cuff endurance on both sides. Reintroduce horizontal pressing and pulling with controlled load. Build the habit of pain monitoring. Avoid any position that loads the right shoulder above 90 degrees of elevation or into impingement range.

### Exercise Key for Phase 1

**Scapular & Rotator Cuff Work (performed every session as a warm-up block)**
- Band pull-aparts: 3 × 15, light band, focus on scapular retraction and depression, elbows slightly soft
- Side-lying external rotation, right side: 3 × 15, 1–2 kg dumbbell, elbow pinned to side, move only within pain-free arc
- Prone Y-T-W raises on incline bench (arms below 90 degrees, no overhead): 2 × 10 each letter, bodyweight or 1 kg plates, slow and controlled
- Serratus anterior wall slides: 2 × 10, forearms on wall, slide upward only as far as pain-free, protract at the top

---

### WEEK 1

**Session A**

Warm-up block as above (band pull-aparts, side-lying ER, prone Y-T-W, wall slides). This applies every session in Phase 1 and will be referenced rather than repeated in full.

*Working sets:*
- Seated cable row, neutral grip: 3 × 12 at RPE 6. Cue: initiate with scapular retraction before elbow drive. Keep right shoulder depressed throughout.
- Chest-supported dumbbell row: 3 × 12 each side, right side use a weight 20–30% lighter than left to start. Cue: do not allow the right shoulder to elevate or internally rotate at the top.
- Incline dumbbell press, 30–45 degree incline only (this keeps the shoulder below impingement range): 3 × 12, light load, RPE 5–6. If any catching sensation on the right, reduce incline further or switch to a cable incline press.
- Dumbbell bicep curl, alternating: 3 × 12, standard.
- Tricep pushdown, rope attachment: 3 × 15, RPE 5.
- Dead hang assessment: Hang from bar with both hands for up to 20 seconds. This is assessment only — note any right shoulder discomfort. Do not progress if painful. This is relevant to her climbing goals and will be developed carefully.

**Session B**

Warm-up block.

- Half-kneeling single-arm cable row (elbow below shoulder height): 3 × 12 each side. The half-kneeling position adds anti-rotation demand relevant to climbing.
- Dumbbell floor press: 3 × 12. The floor limits range of motion at the bottom, protecting the anterior capsule. Use equal weight both sides and monitor right shoulder.
- Face pulls, cable at mid-chest height (not above shoulder): 3 × 15, light load, external rotation emphasis at end range. This is one of the most important exercises in the programme for impingement management.
- Hammer curl: 3 × 12.
- Overhead tricep extension: **Omit entirely** — this places the shoulder in a loaded overhead position. Replace with tricep pushdown, straight bar: 3 × 15.
- Farmer's carry, 20 metres × 3: moderate load, focus on right shoulder depression and scapular stability throughout. Excellent for rotator cuff co-contraction.

**Session C**

Warm-up block.

- Lat pulldown, wide grip to upper chest (not behind neck): 3 × 12, RPE 6. The bar comes to the clavicle, not lower. Monitor right shoulder for any impingement arc discomfort.
- Cable chest press, standing or seated, mid-height: 3 × 12. The cable allows a more shoulder-friendly path than a barbell.
- Prone dumbbell row on incline bench: 3 × 12 each side, bilateral setup. This removes the stabilisation demand from the lower body and isolates the upper back.
- Wrist roller or plate pinch: 2 × 60 seconds. Forearm and grip development for climbing.
- Dead hang: attempt 2 × 20 seconds if Session A assessment was pain-free. If not, continue assessment only.

---

### WEEK 2

Repeat the same exercise selection as Week 1. Increase load by the smallest available increment on any exercise where RPE felt below 6 at the end of Week 1. The goal is not to add load aggressively — it is to establish consistent movement quality and pain-free tolerance. Continue logging pain scores. If dead hangs were pain-free in Week 1, progress to 2 × 30 seconds.

---

### WEEK 3

**Progression:** Add one set to the primary pulling movements (seated cable row, chest-supported row, lat pulldown) — now 4 sets each. Maintain 3 sets on pressing movements. Introduce two new exercises:

- Cable external rotation at 0 degrees abduction (elbow at side): 3 × 15 each side, very light load. This directly targets the infraspinatus and teres minor in a safe position.
- Incline dumbbell curl: 3 × 12. The incline position increases the stretch on the bicep long head, which has a direct attachment at the shoulder — keep load conservative and monitor right shoulder.

Remove the floor press and replace with:
- Low incline dumbbell press (30 degrees): 3 × 12. She should now have enough tissue tolerance to manage this if Weeks 1–2 were pain-free.

Dead hang: progress to 3 × 30 seconds if previous weeks were pain-free.

---

### WEEK 4 — Deload Week

**Reduce all working sets by one and reduce load by approximately 20%.** This is not a rest week — it is an active recovery week that allows connective tissue to consolidate the adaptations from Weeks 1–3. Maintain all exercises but reduce volume and intensity.

This is also the first physio check-in week. Before beginning Phase 2, confirm with her physio that she has tolerated Phase 1 without symptom flare, and ask whether any range of motion restrictions have changed. If she has been cleared for greater range, you can begin to cautiously extend the incline press angle in Phase 2. If restrictions remain the same, Phase 2 proceeds as written.

---

## PHASE 2 — Hypertrophy & Pattern Loading (Weeks 5–8)

### Phase 2 Goals
Increase training volume and load through horizontal and low-diagonal planes. Develop the pulling strength and grip endurance that directly transfers to climbing. Begin introducing unilateral pressing on the right side with careful load management. Maintain all rotator cuff and scapular work as warm-up.

The warm-up block evolves in Phase 2:
- Band pull-aparts: 3 × 20 (increase reps, same light band)
- Side-lying ER, right: 3 × 15, progress to 2–3 kg if pain-free
- Prone Y-T-W: 3 × 10 each, add 1.25 kg plates if bodyweight is easy
- Serratus wall slides: 2 × 12
- Add: Scapular push-up (protraction focus): 2 × 15

---

### WEEK 5

**Session A**

Warm-up block (Phase 2 version).

- Barbell bent-over row, pronated grip: 4 × 8, RPE 7. Introduce the barbell here — the horizontal pulling pattern is now well-established. Cue: hinge to approximately 45 degrees, bar to lower sternum, scapulae retract and depress.
- Incline dumbbell press, 45 degrees: 4 × 10, RPE 7. Right side load should now be within 10–15% of left if Phase 1 was pain-free. If any discomfort, maintain the 20–30% differential.
- Face pulls: 4 × 15, increase load slightly from Phase 1.
- Dumbbell hammer curl: 3 × 12, increase load.
- Tricep pushdown, rope: 3 × 15, increase load.
- Dead hang: 3 × 45 seconds, or progress to active scapular depression hangs (pull shoulder blades down while hanging, hold 2 seconds, release) — 3 × 10 reps. This is a key climbing-specific exercise.

**Session B**

Warm-up block.

- Chest-supported T-bar row or machine row: 4 × 10, RPE 7.
- Single-arm dumbbell press, seated: 3 × 10 each side. The single-arm variation allows you to monitor the right side independently. Start right side at RPE 6 maximum.
- Cable row, close neutral grip: 3 × 12.
- Incline dumbbell curl: 3 × 12.
- Tricep dip, assisted or bodyweight with feet on bench (bench dip): **Use bench dip only** — full parallel bar dips place the shoulder in extension and internal rotation under load, which is contraindicated. Monitor right shoulder carefully even with bench dips. If any discomfort, replace with tricep pushdown.
- Farmer's carry: 3 × 30 metres, increase load from Phase 1.

**Session C**

Warm-up block.

- Lat pulldown, neutral grip: 4 × 10, RPE 7. Neutral grip reduces internal rotation demand compared to wide pronated grip.
- Cable fly, low-to-mid cable (cables set at hip height, press forward and slightly upward to chest height): 3 × 15. This is a safe pressing variation that avoids the impingement arc. Do not allow the cables to travel above shoulder height.
- Prone dumbbell row: 4 × 10 each side.
- Wrist roller: 3 × 60 seconds.
- Plate pinch walk: 3 × 20 metres.
- Scapular pull-up (hang from bar, depress and retract scapulae without bending elbows, hold 2 seconds): 3 × 10. This is a direct precursor to full pull-ups and highly relevant to climbing.

---

### WEEKS 6 AND 7

Continue the same exercise selection as Week 5. Apply progressive overload by adding load when RPE drops below 6 on any given set, or by adding one additional set to the primary compound movements (rows and lat pulldown) in Week 7. By Week 7, target 5 sets on the barbell bent-over row and lat pulldown at RPE 7–8.

In Week 7, introduce one new exercise per session:
- **Session A addition:** Chest-to-bar cable row (seated, pull to lower sternum with elbows flared slightly): 3 × 12. This mimics the lock-off position in climbing.
- **Session B addition:** Single-arm cable row in split stance: 3 × 12 each side. Greater anti-rotation demand.
- **Session C addition:** Assisted pull-up or band-assisted pull-up: 3 × 5–8. Only introduce this if scapular pull-ups have been consistently pain-free and her physio has not flagged any concern about the overhead pulling position. The pull-up is a fundamental climbing movement and this is the appropriate time to begin reintroducing it carefully. If there is any right shoulder discomfort, remain on scapular pull-ups.

---

### WEEK 8 — Deload Week

Same protocol as Week 4. Reduce volume by one set per exercise and load by 20%. Second physio check-in this week. Key questions for the physio: Has overhead range improved? Is she cleared for any loaded overhead work? Can pull-up volume increase in Phase 3? The answers will shape Phase 3 programming.

---

## PHASE 3 — Strength Integration (Weeks 9–12)

### Phase 3 Goals
Consolidate strength gains, increase intensity on compound movements, develop the specific pulling and grip strength that will translate directly back to climbing. If the physio has cleared any overhead range, cautiously introduce it. If not, continue to work within the established safe range and maximise strength within it.

The warm-up block in Phase 3 becomes more dynamic:
- Band pull-aparts: 2 × 20 (maintenance)
- Side-lying ER: 2 × 15 (maintenance, increase load if appropriate)
- Prone Y-T-W: 2 × 10 (maintenance)
- Scapular push-up: 2 × 15
- Add: Thoracic spine rotation with arm reach on foam roller: 2 × 10 each side. Thoracic mobility is critical for climbing and helps offload the shoulder.

---

### WEEK 9

**Session A**

Warm-up block (Phase 3 version).

- Barbell bent-over row: 5 × 5, RPE 8. Shift to a strength rep range. Load should be meaningfully heavier than Phase 2.
- Incline dumbbell press, 45 degrees: 4 × 8, RPE 8. Right and left side should now be at parity or within 5% if Phase 2 was well-tolerated.
- Face pulls: 3 × 20, maintain as shoulder health work throughout.
- Weighted hammer curl: 4 × 10.
- Tricep pushdown: 3 × 12, heavier load.
- Active scapular depression hangs: 3 × 12 reps, or progress to 3 × 60-second dead hangs.

**Session B**

Warm-up block.

- Weighted pull-up or band-assisted pull-up: 4 × 5–8. If she has been doing assisted pull-ups in Week 7 without pain, this is the appropriate progression. If she is not yet at bodyweight pull-ups, continue band assistance and focus on quality. Right shoulder monitoring is essential — any catching or pain, return to scapular pull-ups.
- Single-arm dumbbell press, seated: 4 × 8 each side, RPE 7–8.
- Cable row, close grip: 4 × 10.
- Incline dumbbell curl: 4 × 10.
- Bench dip or tricep pushdown: 3 × 15.
- Farmer's carry: 4 × 30 metres, heaviest load to date.

**Session C**

Warm-up block.

- Lat pulldown, neutral grip: 4 × 8, RPE 8.
- Cable fly, low-to-mid: 3 × 15 (maintenance, shoulder health).
- Chest-to-bar cable row: 4 × 10.
- Wrist roller: 4 × 60 seconds.
- Plate pinch: 3 × 30 metres.
- If physio has cleared any overhead range: introduce a single-arm landmine press. The landmine press is the safest overhead pressing variation for impingement because the bar path is diagonal rather than vertical, and the shoulder never reaches full elevation. Start with the right side at RPE 5 only, 3 × 8, and monitor carefully. If not cleared for overhead, replace with a cable chest press at a slightly higher angle than Phase 2.

---

### WEEKS 10 AND 11

Continue Phase 3 exercise selection. Apply progressive overload on all compound movements. In Week 10, add load to the barbell row and pull-up. In Week 11, attempt a personal best on the bent-over row and lat pulldown within pain-free range. Pull-up volume can increase to 5 × 5–8 in Week 11 if Week 10 was pain-free.

In Week 11, introduce one climbing-specific addition per session if all movements have been pain-free:
- **Session A:** Towel pull-up or thick-grip pull-up (wrapping a towel around the bar): 2 × 5. This directly trains the finger flexor and forearm strength used in climbing.
- **Session B:** Single-arm cable row with a pause at full retraction for 2 seconds: 3 × 10 each side. Mimics the lock-off hold in climbing.
- **Session C:** Pinch block deadlift or pinch plate carry: 3 × 20 metres. Develops the pinch grip used on slopers and volumes.

---

### WEEK 12 — Final Week & Reassessment

This is not a deload week. It is a performance and reassessment week. Maintain full training load. At the end of Week 12, conduct a structured reassessment:

**Reassessment metrics to record:**
- Pain scores across all exercises compared to Week 1 baseline
- Load achieved on key lifts (bent-over row, lat pulldown, incline press) compared to Week 1
- Dead hang duration compared to Week 1
- Pull-up capacity (reps at bodyweight or with assistance level)
- Subjective report of right shoulder confidence and function

**Third physio check-in.** Share reassessment data with her physio. Discuss return-to-climbing timeline, any remaining restrictions, and whether a further strength phase or a climbing-specific conditioning phase is the appropriate next step.

## Nutrition Considerations

You did not specify a nutrition brief, so the following is a general framework appropriate for a recreational athlete in a strength-building programme with an injury history.

**Protein.** For muscle protein synthesis and connective tissue repair, target 1.6–2.0 grams of protein per kilogram of bodyweight per day. Distribute this across three to four meals rather than concentrating it in one sitting. Sources should include complete proteins — meat, fish, eggs, dairy, or well-combined plant sources.

**Collagen and vitamin C.** There is emerging evidence that 15 grams of hydrolysed collagen taken with 50 mg of vitamin C approximately 30–60 minutes before training sessions that involve the shoulder may support tendon and ligament remodelling. This is particularly relevant in the context of an impingement that is still in the rehabilitation phase. This is a supplement recommendation to discuss with her GP or physio, not a prescription.

**Energy availability.** Ensure she is not in a significant caloric deficit during this programme. Tissue repair and strength adaptation both require adequate energy. If she is also managing body composition goals, a very modest deficit of no more than 200–300 calories below maintenance is appropriate — a larger deficit will compromise recovery and potentially slow her physio progress.

**Hydration.** Adequate hydration supports synovial fluid production and joint health. A practical target is pale yellow urine throughout the day.

---

## Recovery Considerations

**Sleep.** Seven to nine hours per night is the single most important recovery variable. Tissue repair, motor learning, and pain modulation are all significantly impaired by sleep restriction. If she reports poor sleep, this warrants a conversation before attributing slow progress to training variables.

**Between-session shoulder care.** On rest days, she should continue any home exercise programme prescribed by her physio. The two programmes should complement, not compete with, each other — hence the importance of the physio check-ins.

**Ice versus heat.** In the early weeks, if she experiences any post-session soreness around the right shoulder, ice for 10–15 minutes post-session is appropriate for any acute inflammatory response. Heat before sessions can help with tissue extensibility. If she experiences persistent soreness lasting more than 24 hours after a session, that session's load was too high and should be reduced.

**Climbing.** She should not return to climbing during this programme without explicit physio clearance. When she does return, the first sessions should be slab climbing or easy traversing — nothing that requires dynamic overhead loading, campus boarding, or overhanging routes. The strength she builds here will make her return safer and more effective.

# Nutrition Plan — Body Recomposition
### 29-year-old recreational climber | Upper-body strength programme | 12-week concurrent goal

---

## A Note on Recomposition and Injury Context

Body recomposition — simultaneously reducing fat mass and building lean muscle — is a legitimate and well-supported goal, but it requires a more precise nutritional approach than either a dedicated bulk or cut. For this client, there is an additional layer of complexity: she is repairing connective tissue. A significant caloric deficit impairs tendon and ligament remodelling, reduces synovial fluid production, and slows the physio progress she has spent four months building. The nutrition plan below is therefore built around the smallest effective deficit, high protein to drive muscle protein synthesis, and specific micronutrient and supplement targets that directly support shoulder tissue repair. Recomposition will be slower than a dedicated cut, but it will be sustainable, it will not compromise her recovery, and it will leave her stronger and more resilient when she returns to climbing.

---

## Step 1 — Estimating Her Targets

You have not provided her current weight or body fat percentage, so the figures below use a worked example of **68 kg** to illustrate the calculation method. Adjust every number proportionally once you have her actual measurements.

### Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE)

Using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation for a 29-year-old female at 68 kg and assuming a height of 165 cm:

**Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR):**
(10 × 68) + (6.25 × 165) − (5 × 29) − 161 = **1,520 kcal**

**Activity multiplier:** She is training three sessions per week with this programme, continuing lower-body and cardiovascular work, and is generally active as a recreational climber. A multiplier of **1.55** (moderately active) is appropriate.

**Estimated TDEE:** 1,520 × 1.55 = approximately **2,356 kcal**

### Recomposition Calorie Target

For recomposition, the evidence supports a deficit of **200–300 kcal below TDEE** on training days, with maintenance calories on rest days. This creates a modest weekly deficit without triggering the hormonal and metabolic responses — cortisol elevation, reduced anabolic signalling, impaired collagen synthesis — that accompany larger deficits.

- **Training day target:** approximately 2,050–2,100 kcal
- **Rest day target:** approximately 2,300–2,350 kcal (maintenance)

Do not go below 1,800 kcal on any day. Below this threshold, protein synthesis, immune function, and connective tissue repair are all meaningfully compromised in a woman of her size and activity level.

---

## Step 2 — Macronutrient Targets

### Protein — The Non-Negotiable Priority

Protein is the most important macronutrient variable for recomposition. It drives muscle protein synthesis, preserves lean mass during a deficit, has the highest thermic effect of food (approximately 25–30% of calories from protein are burned in digestion), and provides the amino acid substrates for collagen production in tendons and ligaments.

**Target: 2.2 grams per kilogram of bodyweight per day**

At 68 kg: **150 grams of protein per day**, every day, regardless of whether it is a training or rest day.

This is at the higher end of the evidence-based range and is intentional. Research on simultaneous fat loss and muscle gain consistently shows that higher protein intakes — above the traditional 1.6 g/kg recommendation — produce superior recomposition outcomes, particularly in trained individuals. The additional protein also provides a buffer against the catabolic environment created by the modest caloric deficit.

At 4 kcal per gram, 150 g of protein accounts for **600 kcal**.

### Fat — Hormonal Health and Joint Lubrication

Fat intake should not be reduced aggressively. Dietary fat is required for oestrogen and testosterone production, both of which are critical for muscle protein synthesis and bone density. Omega-3 fatty acids specifically have anti-inflammatory properties that are directly relevant to her impingement. Synovial fluid quality is also influenced by dietary fat intake.

**Target: 1.0–1.2 grams per kilogram of bodyweight per day**

At 68 kg: **68–82 grams of fat per day**

Use **75 grams** as a practical daily target. At 9 kcal per gram, this accounts for **675 kcal**.

Prioritise unsaturated fat sources. Aim for at least two to three servings of oily fish per week for omega-3s, and use olive oil, avocado, nuts, and seeds as primary fat sources. Limit saturated fat to no more than one-third of total fat intake.

### Carbohydrate — Performance Fuel and Recovery

Carbohydrates fill the remaining calorie budget. They are the primary fuel for resistance training, support glycogen replenishment between sessions, and drive the insulin response that shuttles amino acids into muscle tissue post-training.

**Training day carbohydrate calculation:**
2,075 kcal total − 600 kcal (protein) − 675 kcal (fat) = **800 kcal from carbohydrate = 200 grams**

**Rest day carbohydrate calculation:**
2,325 kcal total − 600 kcal (protein) − 675 kcal (fat) = **1,050 kcal from carbohydrate = 262 grams**

Rest days have higher carbohydrate because calories are at maintenance — this supports glycogen replenishment and recovery between training sessions.

### Summary Macro Targets

| Day Type | Calories | Protein | Fat | Carbohydrate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Training day | ~2,075 kcal | 150 g | 75 g | 200 g |
| Rest day | ~2,325 kcal | 150 g | 75 g | 262 g |

## Step 3 — Protein Distribution and Timing

The total daily protein figure matters, but so does how it is distributed. Muscle protein synthesis is maximised when protein is spread across four to five eating occasions rather than concentrated in one or two large meals. Each meal should contain a minimum of **35–40 grams of protein** to maximally stimulate MPS, based on current evidence for women in a resistance training context.

### Daily Protein Distribution Template

**Meal 1 — Breakfast: 35–40 g protein**
This meal sets the tone for the day and should not be skipped. If she trains in the morning, this becomes her pre-training meal and should be consumed 60–90 minutes before the session.

**Meal 2 — Lunch or mid-morning: 35–40 g protein**
A complete protein source with vegetables and a moderate carbohydrate portion.

**Meal 3 — Post-training or afternoon: 35–40 g protein**
The post-training window. Consume within 60 minutes of finishing the session. Prioritise fast-digesting protein (whey, white fish, eggs) and moderate-to-high glycaemic carbohydrates to drive glycogen replenishment and the anabolic insulin response.

**Meal 4 — Dinner: 35–40 g protein**
The largest meal of the day for most people. Include a slow-digesting protein source (casein-rich foods such as cottage cheese, Greek yoghurt, or a casein shake) to support overnight muscle protein synthesis.

**Optional Meal 5 — Pre-bed snack: 20–30 g protein**
If she is struggling to hit protein targets across four meals, a pre-bed casein-rich snack is well-supported by evidence. 40 grams of casein protein before sleep has been shown to increase overnight MPS by approximately 22% compared to a placebo. Cottage cheese, Greek yoghurt, or a casein protein shake are practical options.

## Step 4 — Carbohydrate Timing and Quality

### Peri-Training Carbohydrate Strategy

**Pre-training (60–90 minutes before session):**
Consume 40–60 grams of moderate-to-low glycaemic index carbohydrates. This tops up muscle glycogen without causing a blood sugar spike and crash mid-session. Examples: oats, sweet potato, wholegrain toast, banana.

**Post-training (within 60 minutes):**
Consume 50–70 grams of higher glycaemic index carbohydrates alongside the post-training protein. The elevated insulin response at this time is anabolic and drives nutrient partitioning toward muscle rather than fat storage. Examples: white rice, white potato, rice cakes, fruit, white bread. This is the one time of day when refined carbohydrates are actively useful.

### Carbohydrate Quality on Rest Days

On rest days, all carbohydrates should come from whole food sources — vegetables, legumes, whole grains, fruit. There is no post-training window to exploit, so the insulin-spiking strategy is not appropriate. Distribute carbohydrates evenly across meals and prioritise fibre-rich sources to support gut health and satiety.

### Fibre Target

Aim for **25–35 grams of dietary fibre per day**. Adequate fibre supports the gut microbiome, which has emerging links to inflammation regulation — relevant to her impingement — and helps manage appetite during the modest caloric deficit.

## Step 5 — Fat Quality and Omega-3 Strategy

### Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Shoulder Inflammation

This deserves specific attention given her injury context. EPA and DHA — the long-chain omega-3 fatty acids found in oily fish and fish oil — have well-documented anti-inflammatory effects. In the context of subacromial impingement, which involves bursal inflammation and rotator cuff tendon irritation, adequate omega-3 intake is a meaningful dietary intervention, not merely a general health recommendation.

**Dietary sources:** Aim for two to three servings of oily fish per week — salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring, or trout. Each serving provides approximately 1.5–2.5 grams of combined EPA and DHA.

**Supplementation:** On days without oily fish, supplement with a high-quality fish oil providing **2–3 grams of combined EPA and DHA per day**. If she is vegetarian or vegan, algae-based omega-3 supplements provide the same EPA and DHA directly and are the evidence-based alternative.

### Olive Oil as Primary Cooking Fat

Extra virgin olive oil contains oleocanthal, a compound with COX-inhibiting anti-inflammatory properties similar in mechanism to ibuprofen, though at a much lower potency. Using it as the primary cooking and dressing fat is a low-effort, evidence-adjacent choice that supports the anti-inflammatory dietary pattern.

## Step 6 — Micronutrients for Connective Tissue Repair

These are not optional extras. They are the raw materials her body needs to repair the rotator cuff tendons and bursa that have been irritated by four months of impingement.

### Vitamin C

Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for collagen synthesis. Without adequate vitamin C, the hydroxylation of proline and lysine — the structural amino acids in collagen — cannot occur. The body cannot store vitamin C, so daily intake is required.

**Target: 200–500 mg per day from food and supplementation combined.**

Food sources: bell peppers (one medium red pepper contains approximately 150 mg), citrus fruit, kiwi, strawberries, broccoli, and Brussels sprouts. If dietary intake is inconsistent, supplement with 250 mg of vitamin C daily. As noted in the training programme, taking 50 mg of vitamin C alongside 15 grams of hydrolysed collagen 30–60 minutes before training sessions has specific evidence for enhancing tendon collagen synthesis.

### Vitamin D

Vitamin D deficiency is extremely common in the UK and northern latitudes, and it impairs muscle protein synthesis, bone density, and immune function. In a woman doing resistance training with an injury history, suboptimal vitamin D is a meaningful obstacle to progress.

**Recommendation:** Test serum 25(OH)D levels if possible. In the absence of testing, supplementing with **1,000–2,000 IU of vitamin D3 per day** throughout the programme is a low-risk, high-value intervention. Take with a fat-containing meal for optimal absorption.

### Magnesium

Magnesium is involved in over 300 enzymatic reactions including muscle contraction, protein synthesis, and sleep regulation. Many active women are mildly deficient. Adequate magnesium supports sleep quality — which, as noted in the training programme, is the most important recovery variable.

**Target: 310–320 mg per day** (the RDA for women aged 19–30).

Food sources: dark leafy greens, pumpkin seeds, almonds, dark chocolate, legumes, and whole grains. If dietary intake is insufficient, supplement with **200–300 mg of magnesium glycinate** before bed. Glycinate is the most bioavailable form and has the added benefit of supporting sleep quality.

### Zinc

Zinc is required for protein synthesis, immune function, and wound healing. It is commonly under-consumed in women who limit red meat.

**Target: 8–12 mg per day.**

Food sources: red meat, shellfish (oysters are exceptionally rich), pumpkin seeds, legumes, and dairy. If she avoids red meat and shellfish, a zinc supplement of 10–15 mg per day is appropriate.

### Calcium

Bone density is a long-term concern for active women, particularly those who may have periods of high training load. Adequate calcium intake is foundational.

**Target: 1,000 mg per day from food.**

Food sources: dairy products, fortified plant milks, tinned sardines with bones, tofu set with calcium sulphate, and dark leafy greens. Supplementation is generally not necessary if dairy or fortified alternatives are consumed regularly, and calcium supplements in isolation carry some cardiovascular risk concerns — food sources are strongly preferred.

## Step 7 — Hydration

Hydration directly affects joint health through its role in synovial fluid production and cartilage lubrication. It also affects training performance, cognitive function, and appetite regulation — mild dehydration of 1–2% of body weight meaningfully impairs strength output.

**Daily target:** A practical starting point is **35 ml per kilogram of bodyweight per day**, which at 68 kg gives approximately **2.4 litres**. Add 500–750 ml for each training session.

**Practical guidance:** Begin each day with 500 ml of water before coffee or food. Carry a 750 ml bottle and aim to refill it three times across the day. Urine should be pale straw yellow by mid-morning. Dark urine at any point in the day indicates under-hydration.

**Electrolytes:** On training days, particularly if she sweats heavily, ensure adequate sodium, potassium, and magnesium intake. A pinch of sea salt in her pre-training water or a low-sugar electrolyte tablet is a practical solution rather than relying on sports drinks.

The following supplements are evidence-supported, relevant to her specific goals, and low-risk. They are listed in order of priority.

**Tier 1 — High priority, strong evidence:**

1. **Whey protein isolate or concentrate:** Use to hit daily protein targets if whole food intake falls short. 25–30 grams per serving. Post-training is the most useful timing. Not necessary if she consistently hits 150 g from food.

It increases phosphocreatine availability, directly improving strength output in the 1–10 rep range, and has emerging evidence for supporting tendon health and reducing inflammation. There is no loading phase required at this dose. It is safe, inexpensive, and effective. Many women are hesitant about creatine due to misconceptions about water retention — the intracellular water retention it causes is within muscle cells and is associated with improved muscle function, not subcutaneous bloating.

3. **Fish oil (EPA + DHA):** 2–3 grams of combined EPA and DHA per day on days without oily fish, as described above.

4. **Vitamin D3:** 1,000–2,000 IU per day with a fat-containing meal.

**Tier 2 — Moderate priority, good evidence in context:**

5. **Hydrolysed collagen + vitamin C:** 15 grams of hydrolysed collagen with 50 mg vitamin C, taken 30–60 minutes before training sessions. The evidence base for this specific protocol — developed largely by Keith Baar's research group — shows increased collagen synthesis in tendons and ligaments when this combination is taken before exercise that loads the relevant tissue. Given her impingement history, this is a meaningful addition.

6. **Magnesium glycinate:** 200–300 mg before bed if dietary intake is insufficient.

7. **Casein protein:** If she struggles to hit protein targets and wants a pre-bed option, a casein shake is a practical solution.

**Tier 3 — Optional, context-dependent:**

8. **Zinc:** 10–15 mg per day if red meat and shellfish intake is low.

9. **Caffeine:** 3–6 mg per kilogram of bodyweight consumed 45–60 minutes before training sessions has strong evidence for improving strength, endurance, and pain tolerance. At 68 kg, this is approximately 200–400 mg — one to two strong coffees. This is not a supplement she needs to purchase; her existing coffee habit, if she has one, can be strategically timed. Avoid caffeine within six hours of sleep.

## Step 10 — Phase-by-Phase Nutrition Adjustments

The nutrition plan is not static across 12 weeks. It should evolve in parallel with the training phases.

**Weeks 1–4 (Foundation Phase):** Prioritise hitting protein targets and establishing the eating pattern above all else. Do not worry about perfect macro tracking in the first two weeks — focus on food quality and protein consistency. Introduce the collagen + vitamin C protocol from Day 1. **Weeks 5–8 (Hypertrophy Phase):** Training volume and intensity are increasing. Ensure carbohydrate intake on training days is consistently at target — this is not the time to under-fuel sessions. If she is not seeing any body composition change after four weeks, reduce rest day calories by 100 kcal (from carbohydrates, not protein or fat) before making any other adjustments.

**Weeks 9–12 (Strength Phase):** Intensity is at its highest. Maintain training day calories at target. If she has been making good recomposition progress, consider a brief two-week maintenance phase at the end of Week 10 — eating at full TDEE — before the final two weeks. This metabolic reset can improve hormonal signalling and training performance for the final push.

## Progress Monitoring

Body recomposition is notoriously difficult to track with the scale alone, because muscle gain and fat loss can offset each other, producing little change in total weight while significant changes in body composition occur. Use multiple metrics:

**Weekly:** Body weight, measured on the same day, at the same time, under the same conditions (morning, post-toilet, pre-food). Average across the week rather than reacting to daily fluctuations.

**Every four weeks:** Circumference measurements — waist, hips, upper arm (both sides), and thigh. Changes in these measurements are more informative than scale weight for recomposition.

**Every four weeks:** Progress photographs in consistent lighting and clothing.

**Ongoing:** Training performance. Strength gains on key lifts are the most reliable indicator that muscle is being built. If she is getting stronger while weight is stable or slightly decreasing, recomposition is working.

**Expected rate of progress:** Realistic recomposition produces approximately 0.5–1 kg of fat loss and 0.5–1 kg of muscle gain per month in a well-trained individual following a structured programme. In a relative beginner to structured resistance training — which she effectively is, given her climbing background — the muscle gain side of this equation may be faster in the first 8–12 weeks due to novice adaptation. Do not set expectations based on scale weight alone.

This plan is built on estimated figures and general evidence-based principles. It is not a substitute for assessment by a registered dietitian, particularly given her injury context. If she has any history of disordered eating, the calorie and macro tracking approach described here should be discussed carefully and may need to be modified toward a more intuitive, food-quality-focused approach. If she has any diagnosed medical conditions affecting metabolism, digestion, or hormonal function, those must be factored in by an appropriate clinician before implementing this plan.

# Cardiovascular Training Programme
### 2 sessions per week | Goal: Return to long climbing days | Integrated with 12-week upper-body strength programme

---

## Framing the Cardio Goal Correctly

Long climbing days are a specific physiological demand that most generic cardio programmes do not address well. A full day at the crag or an indoor endurance session involves sustained low-to-moderate intensity effort across six to eight hours, repeated bouts of grip and upper-body exertion separated by rest periods of variable length, significant time on your feet on uneven terrain, a meaningful carrying load (pack, rope, gear), and the mental fatigue that accumulates over a long day and begins to affect movement quality and decision-making by the afternoon. The cardiovascular system underpinning all of this is primarily **aerobic base capacity** — the ability to sustain moderate effort for extended periods without accumulating fatigue debt — combined with the ability to recover quickly between hard efforts, which in climbing terms means recovering between routes or boulder problems.

The two weekly sessions are therefore not interchangeable. One session builds **aerobic base** — long, low-intensity, sustainable effort that develops mitochondrial density, cardiac stroke volume, and fat oxidation capacity. The other builds **aerobic power and recovery speed** — the ability to push harder and recover faster, which translates to getting back on the wall sooner after a hard pitch. Together they address the full physiological profile of a long climbing day.

---

## Constraints and Integration Principles

Before laying out the programme, the following constraints shape every decision.

**Shoulder protection.** The two most common cardio modalities — running and cycling — are both appropriate for her because neither loads the shoulder. Rowing, ski erg, and assault bike are excluded from primary programming because all three involve significant shoulder drive and could aggravate the right subacromial impingement, particularly under fatigue. They may be reintroduced cautiously in Phase 3 if her physio clears greater shoulder loading, and this is noted where relevant.

**Recovery budget.** She is already doing three upper-body strength sessions per week. Adding two cardio sessions brings her to five training days. This is manageable but leaves no room for additional stress. The cardio sessions must be placed carefully in the weekly schedule to avoid compounding fatigue on strength training days, and total weekly load must be monitored. If at any point she reports persistent fatigue, disrupted sleep, or declining strength performance, the cardio volume is reduced before the strength volume.

**Weekly schedule template.** The following structure distributes training stress across the week without stacking hard sessions back to back:

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Strength Session A |
| Tuesday | Cardio Session 1 (aerobic base) |
| Wednesday | Strength Session B |
| Thursday | Rest or light activity |
| Friday | Strength Session C |
| Saturday | Cardio Session 2 (aerobic power / recovery) |
| Sunday | Full rest |

Thursday is a genuine rest day or very light activity only — a walk, gentle mobility work, or her physio home programme. It is not a training day. Sunday is full rest. This structure ensures she never does more than two consecutive training days and always has 48 hours between the Saturday cardio session and Monday strength session.

If her schedule requires adjustment, the non-negotiable rules are: do not place a hard cardio session the day before a strength session, and do not place two hard sessions on consecutive days.

---

## Intensity Framework

All cardio sessions use a **three-zone model** based on heart rate. This is simpler and more practically useful than five-zone models for a recreational athlete without access to lactate testing.

**Zone 1 — Easy aerobic (50–65% of maximum heart rate)**
Conversational pace. You can speak in full sentences without effort. This is recovery-level intensity and is used for warm-ups, cool-downs, and active recovery days.

**Zone 2 — Aerobic base (65–75% of maximum heart rate)**
You can speak in short sentences but would not choose to hold a long conversation. Breathing is elevated but controlled. This is the primary training zone for aerobic base development and is where the majority of long climbing day fitness is built. It feels almost too easy, which is why most people avoid it — but it is the zone where mitochondrial adaptations, fat oxidation, and cardiac efficiency are maximised.

**Zone 3 — Aerobic power (75–85% of maximum heart rate)**
Speaking is uncomfortable. Breathing is heavy. This is sustainable for minutes, not hours. Used in interval work to develop lactate threshold and recovery speed.

**Maximum heart rate estimate:** 220 minus age = 191 bpm for a 29-year-old. This is an estimate with meaningful individual variation. If she has access to a heart rate monitor — which is strongly recommended for this programme — she can refine her zones over the first two weeks by feel and observation.

**Practical heart rate targets:**

| Zone | % Max HR | Estimated BPM (29-year-old) |
|---|---|---|
| Zone 1 | 50–65% | 96–124 bpm |
| Zone 2 | 65–75% | 124–143 bpm |
| Zone 3 | 75–85% | 143–162 bpm |

---

## Modality Selection and Rationale

**Primary modality for Session 1 (aerobic base): Incline treadmill walking or outdoor hiking**

This is the single most specific cardio modality for returning to long climbing days. It directly replicates the approach walk, the descent, and the sustained low-intensity locomotion that bookends every climbing day. Incline treadmill walking at 4–6 km/h at 8–12% gradient keeps heart rate solidly in Zone 2 without the impact stress of running, is completely shoulder-safe, and builds the hip flexor, glute, and calf endurance that fatigues on long mountain days. It is also mentally accessible — she can listen to a podcast or music, which matters for adherence on a 45–75 minute session.

Running is an acceptable alternative if she prefers it and has no lower-body injury history. The programming logic is identical — the target is Zone 2 heart rate for the prescribed duration.

**Primary modality for Session 2 (aerobic power): Cycling — stationary bike or outdoor**

Cycling is the best shoulder-safe option for interval work. It allows precise effort control, the resistance can be adjusted instantly, and the seated position removes any shoulder stabilisation demand. A stationary bike is preferable in the early phases for consistency and safety. Outdoor cycling is appropriate from Phase 2 onward if she is comfortable and the terrain is manageable.

**Secondary modalities (can substitute either session from Phase 2 onward):**
- Stair climber or StepMill: excellent climbing-specific modality, replicates the vertical gain of approach walks and multi-pitch climbing. Shoulder-safe. Can replace Session 1 from Week 5.
- Elliptical: lower specificity but shoulder-safe and low-impact. Acceptable substitute if she has any lower-body soreness.
- Swimming: shoulder-dependent and therefore excluded until physio clearance for full shoulder loading. Do not substitute swimming without explicit physio sign-off.
- Ski erg or rowing: excluded until Phase 3 and only with physio clearance, as noted above.

## PHASE 1 — Weeks 1–4: Building the Aerobic Foundation

### Phase 1 Cardio Goals
Establish the habit of two weekly cardio sessions. Develop comfort and consistency in Zone 2. Build the aerobic base that will support higher intensity work in Phase 2. Keep total session duration modest to avoid compromising recovery from the strength programme.

---

### SESSION 1 — Aerobic Base (Tuesday)
**Modality:** Incline treadmill walk or steady-state run/walk
**Target zone:** Zone 2 throughout (65–75% max HR)

**Week 1:** 35 minutes total
- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up, flat or low incline
- 25 minutes Zone 2, incline 8–10%, speed 4.5–5.5 km/h (adjust to keep HR in zone)
- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down, reduce incline to flat

**Week 2:** 40 minutes total
- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up
- 30 minutes Zone 2, incline 8–10%
- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

**Week 3:** 45 minutes total
- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up
- 35 minutes Zone 2, incline 10–12%
- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

**Week 4 (deload):** 30 minutes total
- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up
- 20 minutes Zone 2, incline 8%
- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

**Coaching note for Session 1:** The most common error in Zone 2 training is going too hard. If she is consistently above 143 bpm, slow down or reduce the incline. The adaptation happens in the zone, not above it. It should feel almost frustratingly easy for the first few weeks. That is correct.

---

### SESSION 2 — Aerobic Power Introduction (Saturday)

**Target zone:** Zone 2 base with short Zone 3 introductions

In Phase 1, Session 2 is not yet a full interval session. The goal is to introduce the feeling of Zone 3 effort and begin developing the aerobic power system without creating excessive fatigue in the first month.

- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up

- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up

- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up
- 15 minutes Zone 2 only, no Zone 3 efforts
- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

## PHASE 2 — Weeks 5–8: Developing Aerobic Power and Duration

### Phase 2 Cardio Goals
Extend Session 1 duration toward the 60-minute range that begins to replicate the sustained effort of a long climbing day. Introduce structured interval work in Session 2 to develop lactate threshold and recovery speed. Begin introducing climbing-specific modalities.

- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up
- 45 minutes Zone 2, incline 10–12%, backpack for final 25 minutes
- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

**Week 7:** 60 minutes total
- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up
- 50 minutes Zone 2, incline 10–12%, backpack for final 30 minutes
- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

- 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up
- 30 minutes Zone 2, no backpack
- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

A well-fitted pack with a hip belt transfers most of the load to the hips and should not significantly load the shoulder. ### SESSION 2 — Structured Intervals (Saturday)
**Modality:** Stationary bike or outdoor cycling
**Target zone:** Zone 2 base with Zone 3 intervals

Phase 2 Session 2 introduces proper interval structure. The work-to-rest ratios are designed to develop the ability to push hard and recover quickly — directly relevant to recovering between climbing routes.

**Week 5:** 40 minutes total

- 8 minutes Zone 1–2 cool-down

- 8 minutes cool-down (note: reduce warm-up to 4 minutes if total time is a constraint, but do not reduce cool-down)

**Week 7:** 45 minutes total
- 8 minutes warm-up

- 8 minutes cool-down (adjust warm-up to 5 minutes if needed)

- 5 minutes warm-up
- 4 × (2 minutes Zone 3 + 2 minutes Zone 1 recovery), total 16 minutes

- 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down

# Hangboard & Climbing-Specific Preparation
### Integrated into Phases 2 and 3 | Right shoulder impingement protocol | Return-to-climbing goal

---

## Framing This Addition Carefully

Before writing a single set or rep, this section requires a direct conversation with her physio. Hangboard training is compressive loading of the finger flexor tendons, the wrist, the elbow, and — critically — the shoulder. Every hang places the glenohumeral joint in a position of elevation and the rotator cuff under co-contraction demand. For a healthy climber, this is unremarkable. For someone four months into physio for right subacromial impingement, it is a meaningful clinical decision, not a programming one.

The framework below is built on the most conservative possible progression — starting with positions and loads that minimise shoulder involvement and building only as tolerance is demonstrated. But the physio must be informed that hangboard work is being introduced, and their input must be sought before Phase 2 begins. If they advise against it, the hangboard protocol is deferred entirely until clearance is given, and the climbing-specific preparation focuses exclusively on the shoulder-safe elements described later in this section.

With that established, here is the full framework.

---

## The Physiological Demands of Climbing — What We Are Training For

To programme intelligently, it helps to be precise about what long climbing days actually require at a tissue level. The demands can be broken into five categories, each of which maps to a specific training intervention.

**Finger flexor strength and endurance.** The ability to hold edges, crimps, slopers, and pockets is the most obvious limiting factor in climbing performance. This is trained directly on the hangboard and through grip work in the gym.

**Forearm aerobic capacity.** The forearm muscles are small and have limited blood flow relative to their work output. On long climbing days, the ability to recover between routes — to pump down — is largely a function of forearm aerobic capacity. This is trained through high-repetition, low-load hanging and through the cardiovascular base work already in the programme.

**Shoulder girdle stability under load.** Every hang, every pull, every lock-off requires the rotator cuff and scapular stabilisers to maintain a stable glenohumeral joint. This is the area of greatest concern for her and is the primary focus of the strength programme already in place. The hangboard work builds on this foundation.

**Pulling strength and lock-off capacity.** The ability to pull through a move and hold a lock-off position — elbow at 90 degrees or less — is trained through the pull-up and row progressions in the strength programme and through specific lock-off holds on the hangboard.

**Proprioception and movement pattern.** The neuromuscular skill of climbing — reading sequences, weighting feet, moving efficiently — cannot be trained off the wall. This is addressed in the return-to-climbing protocol at the end of this section.

---

## Equipment Requirements

**Hangboard.** A wooden hangboard is strongly preferred over plastic or resin for this protocol. Wood is slightly more forgiving on the finger pulleys and skin, and the texture provides better feedback. A board with a variety of edge depths — 20 mm, 15 mm, and 10 mm edges as a minimum, plus a sloper and a jug — gives enough variety for the full progression. Suitable options include the Beastmaker 1000 or 2000, the Tension Climbing Flash Board, or any comparable wooden board. The board should be mounted at a height that allows a dead hang with feet off the ground and arms fully extended.

**If she does not have access to a hangboard at her gym**, a pull-up bar can substitute for the early phases using towel hangs and open-hand grips on the bar itself. This is a meaningful compromise but workable for Weeks 5–8. From Phase 3, a proper hangboard is strongly recommended.

**Pulley system for assisted hanging.** A simple pulley and weight system — or a commercially available Tension Block or Crimpd Pulley System — allows precise load reduction for the right side. This is essential for the early phases of hangboard work when the right shoulder cannot tolerate full bodyweight loading. If a pulley system is not available, a bathroom scale can be used to measure how much weight she is offloading through her feet during two-footed assisted hangs.

**Fingerboard training log.** Every hangboard session must be logged: grip position, edge depth, hang duration, rest duration, number of sets, load (bodyweight or assisted), and right shoulder pain score before and after. This is not optional — the progression in this protocol is data-driven, and without a log, you cannot make safe decisions about when to advance.

## Grip Position Hierarchy — Shoulder Safety and Injury Risk

Not all grip positions are equal in terms of shoulder loading. The following hierarchy runs from lowest to highest shoulder demand and determines the order in which grip positions are introduced.

**1. Open hand (four-finger drag)**
The safest grip position for both the fingers and the shoulder. The fingers are extended at the first and second joints, with only the third joint flexed. The shoulder is in a relatively neutral position with lower rotator cuff co-contraction demand than crimping. This is the starting position for all hangboard work in this protocol and the grip position used for the longest period.

**2. Half crimp**
The first and second finger joints are flexed to approximately 90 degrees, the third joint is extended. More shoulder involvement than open hand due to the increased forearm tension and the tendency to engage the shoulder girdle more actively. Introduced in Phase 3 only.

**3. Full crimp**
The thumb wraps over the index finger. Highest finger pulley stress of any grip position and the highest shoulder co-contraction demand. Excluded from this protocol entirely. Full crimping is the most common cause of A2 pulley injuries in climbers and is not appropriate for a return-to-climbing programme. She can reintroduce it independently once she is back on the wall and has rebuilt tissue tolerance over several months.

**4. Slopers**
The hand is open and the contact is through the palm and distal pads. Slopers require significant shoulder internal rotation and depression — a position that can be provocative for subacromial impingement. Introduced very cautiously in Phase 3 Week 11 only, and only if the shoulder has been consistently pain-free throughout the programme.

**5. Pinch**
Already included in the strength programme as plate pinch and pinch block work. Not trained on the hangboard in this protocol.

## PHASE 1 (Weeks 1–4) — No Hangboard Work

Phase 1 does not include hangboard training. This is intentional and non-negotiable. The rotator cuff and scapular stabilisers need four weeks of structured gym work before they are asked to manage the specific loading pattern of hanging. Introducing the hangboard too early — before the shoulder has rebuilt its stability foundation — risks a symptom flare that sets back both the physio progress and the training programme.

What Phase 1 does include, already written into the strength programme, is the groundwork for hangboard readiness:

- Dead hangs from a pull-up bar (assessment and progressive duration)
- Scapular depression hangs
- Farmer's carries for rotator cuff co-contraction
- Face pulls and external rotation work for posterior cuff strength
- Wrist roller and plate pinch for forearm and grip conditioning

By the end of Week 4, if dead hangs have been consistently pain-free and her physio check-in is positive, she is ready to begin Phase 2 hangboard work.

**Phase 1 climbing-specific preparation** is limited to the following off-wall work, which can be done on any day including rest days:

*Antagonist finger extensor training:* Using a rubber band or Metolius Grip Saver, perform finger extension exercises — spread fingers against resistance, hold two seconds, release. Three sets of 15 repetitions per hand, every day. This is one of the most neglected and most important injury prevention exercises for climbers. The finger flexors are trained constantly in climbing; the extensors are almost never trained, creating an imbalance that contributes to pulley injuries and elbow tendinopathy. Starting this in Week 1 builds the habit and the tissue tolerance before any flexor loading begins.

*Wrist mobility and forearm flexibility:* Two minutes of wrist circles, wrist flexion and extension stretches, and forearm pronation/supination at the end of every training session. Thirty seconds each direction. This takes two minutes and meaningfully reduces the risk of wrist and elbow issues when climbing volume increases.

## PHASE 2 (Weeks 5–8) — Hangboard Introduction

### Phase 2 Hangboard Goals
Introduce hanging in the safest possible position — open hand, assisted load, short duration — and establish the tissue tolerance and movement pattern that Phase 3 will build on. Develop forearm aerobic capacity through high-repetition, low-intensity hanging. Begin to differentiate right and left side loading.

### Hangboard Session Structure in Phase 2

Hangboard work is added to **Strength Session C** (Friday) in Phase 2. It replaces the wrist roller and plate pinch at the end of that session — those exercises are not lost, they are moved to Session A or B. Adding hangboard work to Session C means it follows two days of rest from the previous strength session and precedes the Saturday cardio session, which is shoulder-safe cycling. This is the most recovery-friendly placement in the weekly schedule.

**Total hangboard time in Phase 2:** 15–20 minutes added to the end of Session C.

**Before every hangboard session:**
Complete the standard Phase 2 warm-up block from the strength programme. Then add the following specific hangboard warm-up:

- Finger extensor band work: 2 × 15 each hand
- Wrist circles and forearm stretches: 2 minutes
- Gentle open-hand hang from the jug hold (largest, most comfortable hold on the board): 3 × 10 seconds with 30 seconds rest, both hands, feet lightly touching the floor to reduce load. This is a warm-up hang, not a working set.
- Right shoulder pain check: 0–10 scale. Proceed only if 0–1.

---

### WEEK 5 — Hangboard Session (added to Session C)

**Protocol: Assisted open-hand dead hangs, jug hold**

Use the pulley system to reduce load. Start with approximately **50% of bodyweight** on the hangboard — meaning the pulley system is supporting roughly half her weight. If she weighs 68 kg, she is hanging approximately 34 kg through her hands. This is conservative by design.

- 6 × 10-second hangs, open hand on jug
- 50 seconds rest between hangs
- Both hands on the same hold, feet off the ground, pulley assisting
- Focus: scapular depression throughout the hang (actively pull shoulder blades down, do not hang passively), neutral spine, relaxed legs
- Right shoulder pain score after each hang: log it

**Why 10 seconds?** Ten-second hangs at low intensity primarily train the aerobic energy system of the forearm — the oxidative capacity that determines how quickly she pumps down between routes. They are also short enough that any shoulder discomfort is immediately apparent and the set can be stopped without having committed to a long effort.

**Coaching cue for scapular depression:** Before each hang, stand under the bar, reach up, and before taking weight, actively pull the shoulder blades down and together. Hold that position as you take your feet off the ground. The hang should feel like the scapular depression exercises she has been doing in the strength programme — because it is the same movement, just loaded differently.

---

### WEEK 6 — Hangboard Session

**Protocol: Assisted open-hand dead hangs, jug and 20 mm edge**

- Jug hangs: 4 × 10 seconds, 50 seconds rest, same assisted load as Week 5
- 20 mm edge hangs, open hand: 4 × 7 seconds, 60 seconds rest, same assisted load
- The 20 mm edge is a meaningful step up from the jug. The contact area is smaller, the finger flexors work harder, and the shoulder co-contraction demand increases slightly. Monitor right shoulder carefully on the first set.
- If the 20 mm edge causes any right shoulder discomfort, return to jug hangs only and do not progress the edge depth this week.
- Total hanging volume: 8 sets

---

### WEEK 7 — Hangboard Session

**Protocol: Reduced assistance, open hand, jug and 20 mm edge**

Reduce the pulley assistance so she is now hanging approximately **65–70% of bodyweight** — the pulley is supporting 30–35% rather than 50%.

- Jug hangs: 3 × 10 seconds, 50 seconds rest
- 20 mm edge hangs: 5 × 7 seconds, 60 seconds rest
- Add: **Unilateral assessment hang, right hand only, jug hold, feet on floor.** This is not a working set. It is an assessment. Have her place her right hand on the jug, take approximately 30–40% of her bodyweight through the hand (feet still on floor taking the majority), and hold for 5 seconds. Note any right shoulder discomfort. This assessment determines whether unilateral right-side hanging is appropriate in Phase 3.
- Total hanging volume: 8 sets plus assessment

---

### WEEK 8 — Deload (Hangboard)

- Jug hangs only: 4 × 10 seconds, 60 seconds rest, return to 50% bodyweight assistance
- No edge work this week
- Repeat the unilateral right-hand assessment from Week 7 and compare notes
- This is also the second physio check-in week. Share the hangboard assessment data — specifically the right shoulder pain scores during hanging — with her physio. Ask explicitly whether unilateral hanging and reduced assistance are appropriate for Phase 3.

---

### Phase 2 Climbing-Specific Preparation (Off Hangboard)

In addition to the hangboard work, the following climbing-specific elements are integrated into Phase 2.

**Footwork and balance training (Thursday light activity day):**
Introduce single-leg balance work on an unstable surface — a balance board, a BOSU ball, or simply standing on one leg on a folded mat. Three sets of 30 seconds each side. This develops the proprioceptive sensitivity and ankle stability that underpins good footwork on the wall. Poor footwork is the most common technical fault in recreational climbers returning after a break, and it places additional load on the upper body to compensate.

**Hip flexibility and hip-to-wall mobility:**
Two to three minutes of hip flexor stretching, pigeon pose or figure-four stretch, and hip external rotation work at the end of every training session. The ability to drop a hip toward the wall — the hip-in technique — is fundamental to efficient movement on vertical and overhanging terrain. Climbers who lack hip mobility compensate with upper body strength, which is exactly what she cannot afford to do with a compromised shoulder.

**Visualisation and route reading:**
On rest days, spend 10 minutes watching climbing footage — YouTube, Instagram, or competition footage — with the specific intention of reading sequences rather than watching passively. Identify where the climber places their feet before their hands, where they rest, how they use their hips. This is a genuine training stimulus for the motor planning systems involved in climbing and costs nothing in physical recovery.

## PHASE 3 (Weeks 9–12) — Hangboard Progression and Return-to-Climbing Preparation

### Phase 3 Hangboard Goals
Progress toward bodyweight hanging on both hands. Introduce the 15 mm edge. Begin unilateral hanging on the right side with careful load management. Introduce lock-off holds. By Week 12, she should be physically and technically prepared for a supervised return to easy climbing.

### Hangboard Session Structure in Phase 3

Hangboard work moves to its own dedicated slot in Phase 3 — it is no longer appended to Session C. It becomes a **15–25 minute standalone session on Thursday**, which was previously a rest or light activity day. This reflects the increased importance of climbing-specific preparation in the final phase and allows the hangboard work to be done fresh rather than fatigued from a strength session.

The Thursday hangboard session replaces the light activity on that day. Total weekly training days remain at five (three strength, two cardio, one hangboard). Sunday remains full rest.

**Updated weekly schedule for Phase 3:**

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Strength Session A |
| Tuesday | Cardio Session 1 |
| Wednesday | Strength Session B |
| Thursday | Hangboard session |
| Friday | Strength Session C |
| Saturday | Cardio Session 2 |
| Sunday | Full rest |

**Before every Phase 3 hangboard session:**
- Finger extensor band work: 2 × 15 each hand
- Wrist and forearm mobility: 2 minutes
- Jug hang warm-up: 3 × 10 seconds, 60 seconds rest, 70% bodyweight (light assistance)
- Right shoulder pain check: 0–10. Proceed only if 0–1.

---

### WEEK 9 — Hangboard Session

**Protocol: Near-bodyweight bilateral hangs, open hand, jug and 20 mm edge. Introduction of 15 mm edge.**

Reduce pulley assistance to **15–20% of bodyweight** — she is now hanging 80–85% of her bodyweight. This is a significant step and should only be taken if Week 7 and the Week 8 deload were consistently pain-free.

- Jug hangs: 3 × 10 seconds, 50 seconds rest, 80–85% bodyweight
- 20 mm edge, open hand: 4 × 7 seconds, 60 seconds rest, 80–85% bodyweight
- 15 mm edge, open hand: 3 × 5 seconds, 75 seconds rest, 80–85% bodyweight. The 15 mm edge is a meaningful challenge. Five seconds is short enough to be safe but long enough to assess tolerance. If any finger discomfort (not shoulder — finger pulley pain is a separate concern and must be taken seriously), stop immediately and return to the 20 mm edge.
- **Unilateral right-hand hang, jug, feet partially on floor:** 3 × 5 seconds, 90 seconds rest. She should be taking approximately 50–60% of her bodyweight through the right hand, with the remainder through her feet. This is the first time the right shoulder is loaded unilaterally in a hanging position. Log pain scores meticulously.

---

### WEEK 10 — Hangboard Session

**Protocol: Full bodyweight bilateral hangs. Increased unilateral right-side loading. Introduction of lock-off holds.**

Remove pulley assistance entirely for bilateral hangs on the jug. She is now hanging full bodyweight on two hands for the first time in this programme.

- Jug hangs, full bodyweight: 4 × 10 seconds, 50 seconds rest
- 20 mm edge, full bodyweight: 4 × 7 seconds, 60 seconds rest
- 15 mm edge, full bodyweight: 3 × 5 seconds, 75 seconds rest
- Unilateral right-hand hang, jug, 60–70% bodyweight through right hand: 3 × 5 seconds, 90 seconds rest. Increase the proportion of weight through the right hand compared to Week 9.
- **Lock-off introduction:** From the jug hold, hang at full extension, then pull up to 90-degree elbow flexion and hold for 3 seconds before lowering slowly. This is a lock-off hold — one of the most important positions in climbing. Perform 3 × 3 reps, both hands, full bodyweight. The lowering phase should take 3–4 seconds. Right shoulder monitoring is critical here — the lock-off position loads the rotator cuff differently from a dead hang and may be provocative. If any right shoulder discomfort, remove the lock-off and continue with dead hangs only.

---

### WEEK 11 — Hangboard Session

**Protocol: Full bodyweight, edge progression, unilateral development, sloper introduction.**

- Jug hangs: 3 × 10 seconds, 50 seconds rest (maintenance)
- 20 mm edge: 4 × 10 seconds, 60 seconds rest. Increase duration from 7 to 10 seconds.
- 15 mm edge: 4 × 7 seconds, 70 seconds rest
- Unilateral right-hand hang, jug, 70–80% bodyweight through right hand: 4 × 5 seconds, 90 seconds rest
- Lock-off holds: 3 × 3 reps if Week 10 was pain-free
- **Sloper introduction (conditional):** Only if the right shoulder has been consistently pain-free across all Phase 3 sessions and physio has not flagged any concern. Sloper hang on the board's sloper hold, both hands, 80% bodyweight: 3 × 5 seconds, 75 seconds rest. Slopers require shoulder internal rotation and are the most shoulder-demanding grip position in this protocol. If there is any doubt, skip this and add it post-programme.

---

### WEEK 12 — Hangboard Session (Final Assessment)

**Protocol: Performance assessment and programme close.**

This session is a structured assessment of where she has arrived, not a push for new records.

- Jug hang, full bodyweight: maximum comfortable duration, both hands. Log the time.
- 20 mm edge, full bodyweight: maximum comfortable duration, open hand. Log the time.
- 15 mm edge, full bodyweight: maximum comfortable duration, open hand. Log the time.
- Unilateral right-hand jug hang, 80% bodyweight: maximum comfortable duration. Log the time.
- Compare all figures to Week 5 baseline. The improvement in hang duration and load tolerance is a concrete measure of the tissue adaptation that has occurred across eight weeks of hangboard work.

## Return-to-Climbing Protocol

This is the section that ties everything together. The return to climbing is not a single event — it is a structured progression across several sessions that prioritises movement quality, shoulder monitoring, and confidence rebuilding over performance. The following protocol is designed to begin after Week 12, assuming the physio has given clearance for climbing.

### Pre-Return Checklist

Before she sets foot on a wall, the following criteria should be met. These are not arbitrary — each one maps to a specific demand of climbing.

**Shoulder criteria:**
- Zero pain during all Phase 3 hangboard sessions for a minimum of two consecutive weeks
- Zero pain during pull-ups (or band-assisted pull-ups) for a minimum of two consecutive weeks
- Physio has explicitly cleared return to climbing
- Right shoulder external rotation strength is at least 90% of left side (your physio contact can assess this)

**Strength criteria:**
- Can complete 3 × 5 pull-ups (bodyweight or band-assisted) without right shoulder discomfort
- Can dead hang for at least 30 seconds on both hands at full bodyweight
- Can complete the lock-off hold protocol from Week 10 without discomfort

**Cardiovascular criteria:**
- Has completed at least two Session 1 cardio sessions of 60 minutes or more in Phase 3
- Resting heart rate has declined from baseline (indicating aerobic adaptation)

**Technical criteria:**
- Has been doing the footwork and balance training consistently through Phase 2 and 3
- Has been doing the hip mobility work consistently

If any shoulder criterion is not met, climbing is deferred and the physio is consulted. The other criteria can be partially unmet — she does not need to be perfect on pull-ups or hang duration to return to easy climbing — but the shoulder criteria are non-negotiable.

---

**Location:** Indoor climbing wall, bouldering area
**Duration:** 45–60 minutes including warm-up
**Grade:** Well below her pre-injury level — if she was climbing V4–V5 before injury, start at V0–V1

**Structure:**

Warm-up (15 minutes):
- 5 minutes of walking and light movement

- Use only jug holds and large features — no small edges, no crimping, no slopers

- Hang from jugs at full extension for 2 × 20 seconds

# Phase 3 Intensity Overhaul
### Peaking for Week 12 Climbing Trip | Full Programme Integration

---

## Reframing Phase 3 Completely

Everything written previously about Phase 3 being a consolidation phase is now superseded. She has a hard deadline — a climbing trip at the end of Week 12 — and that changes the entire logic of the final four weeks. Instead of a gradual strength integration block followed by a comfortable reassessment week, Phase 3 becomes a **peaking block** with a deliberate taper in the final week so she arrives at the trip physically fresh, neurologically primed, and psychologically confident.

This is a meaningful shift and it carries real risk that you need to communicate to her clearly before beginning. Peaking blocks push intensity to levels that are not sustainable beyond four weeks. They accumulate fatigue deliberately in Weeks 9–11 and then dissipate that fatigue in Week 12 through reduced volume. If the taper is executed correctly, she will feel stronger in Week 12 than at any point in the programme. If the taper is skipped or shortened — because she feels good and wants to keep training hard — she will arrive at the trip fatigued and underperform. The taper is not optional.

The shoulder caveat from every previous section applies here with greater force. Increased intensity means increased load on the right shoulder. The physio check-in at Week 8 is now a critical gate. If she has not been cleared for the loading levels described in Phase 3, the intensity targets below must be moderated. Peaking for a climbing trip on a shoulder that is not ready will not produce the outcome she wants. It will produce a flare-up that cancels the trip entirely.

---

## Phase 3 Peaking Architecture

The four weeks of Phase 3 follow a **3-1 loading pattern** with a twist: the deload in Week 12 is not a standard 20% volume reduction. It is a full **performance taper** — volume drops sharply while intensity is maintained or slightly increased, so the neuromuscular system stays primed while accumulated fatigue clears.

| Week | Loading Phase | Primary Stimulus | Fatigue Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| Week 9 | Intensification 1 | Maximal strength, heavy compound work | High |
| Week 10 | Intensification 2 | Peak volume + intensity, climbing specificity | Very high |
| Week 11 | Overreach | Highest intensity of programme, deliberate overreach | Maximum |
| Week 12 | Performance taper | Volume drops 50–60%, intensity maintained | Dissipating → Fresh |

**A note on deliberate overreach in Week 11.** Functional overreaching — pushing training stress beyond normal recovery capacity for a short, defined period before a taper — is a well-established peaking strategy used in strength sports, endurance sports, and climbing. It works because the supercompensation response during the subsequent taper produces fitness and strength levels above the pre-overreach baseline. It requires that the overreach period is genuinely short (one week maximum), that the taper follows immediately and without compromise, and that nutrition and sleep are prioritised aggressively during both the overreach and the taper. If any of these conditions are not met, overreaching becomes overtraining, which is the opposite of what she needs before a climbing trip.
